title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A transcription service allegedly joined workplace video calls and recorded conversations without obtaining consent from all participants, then used those recordings to train its AI systems. The service's privacy policy mentioned consent options, but the lawsuit claims users were deceived about how their conversations would be shared and used. This represents a failure to obtain meaningful informed consent before processing sensitive workplace audio.

The core issue is whether the system was deployed with adequate safeguards for a multi-party consent environment. Recording calls on platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams involves participants who may not have agreed to be recorded or to have their words used for model training. The failure occurred in how the service managed participant notification and opt-in, not in the transcription itself.

It is not established whether Otter's de-identification process actually failed to protect sensitive information, or whether the company knowingly deceived users. The lawsuit and court's decision to allow claims to proceed are allegations and procedural rulings, not findings of fact about what occurred or what harm resulted.

summary:
# Summary

A federal class-action lawsuit filed in California alleges that Otter.ai, a popular AI transcription service with 25 million users, secretly records workplace conversations without proper consent and uses them to train its systems. The suit, brought by Justin Brewer, claims that Otter's software joins virtual meetings on platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams without asking all participants for permission and fails to adequately alert them that recordings will be shared with the company. While Otter's privacy policy mentions consent options, the lawsuit argues that many users are deceived about how their conversations are being used.

The lawsuit claims Otter violates state and federal privacy laws and seeks to represent others in California affected by the practice. Otter argues it de-identifies audio before using it for AI training, but the suit questions whether this process actually protects confidential information. Recent reports have highlighted privacy concerns, including incidents where sensitive business discussions were shared without full participant awareness and potential risks involving discussions with sources in sensitive situations.
